turn1.explanation: The unit fires on clause- and sentence-boundary punctuation (commas, periods, semicolons) and is strongest when the surrounding document is about ships, boats or maritime topics, so it looks like a nautical-context signal read out at punctuation tokens. Weaker activations appear on list and sentence punctuation in documents with little or no visible maritime content, such as news broadcasting or a radiology report.
turn1.evidence: Nearly all top examples are boat or ship documents (SeaArk boats, power ships, a cruise ship, a historic ship list, flying boats, V.Ships, 'Anchor' electronics), and they fire on punctuation far from any ship word while content tokens stay near zero. Middle examples include other ship contexts (a Stargate ship, a cargo ship, a rig in Ship Shoal, a pirate ship) at lower values, and non-nautical punctuation reaches only about 1.4 to 2.8.
turn1.missing_data: Activations on the same punctuation-dense text with and without maritime words earlier in the document, plus full-document windows for the non-nautical middle examples, to test whether the topic modulation is real.
